content: The Flexner Report is a comprehensive study of medical education in the United States and Canada, authored by Abraham Flexner, a professional educator, and published in 1910 under the auspices of the Carnegie Foundation. This report profoundly influenced the structure and standards of modern American medical education and practice. The Flexner Report, also known as Carnegie Foundation Bulletin Number Four, advocated for higher admission and graduation standards in medical schools. It emphasized strict adherence to the principles of mainstream science in both teaching and research. At the time of its publication, many American medical schools failed to meet these standards. Consequently, nearly half of these schools either merged with other institutions or closed entirely. The report also concluded that there were too many medical schools in the United States and that an excessive number of doctors were being trained. In the late 19th century, allopathic medicine emerged as a dominant approach, grounded in antiseptic surgery, the germ theory of infectious disease, and the scientific method, including clinical trials. The American Medical Association (AMA) sought to eliminate medical schools that did not fully commit to allopathic medicine. In 1904, the AMA established the Council on Medical Education (CME) to restructure medical education in the United States. The CME set two key standards: a minimum level of prior education for medical school admission and a medical education curriculum consisting of two years of training in human anatomy and physiology, followed by two years of clinical work in a teaching hospital. In 1908, the CME requested the Carnegie Foundation to survey American medical education to promote its reformist agenda and accelerate the closure of substandard medical schools. Henry Pritchett, the president of the Carnegie Foundation and a strong advocate for medical school reform, selected Flexner to conduct the survey. At the time, the 155 medical schools in North America varied widely in their curricula, assessment methods, and admission and graduation requirements. Flexner visited all 155 schools and described their shortcomings, including excessive reliance on lectures, inadequate clinical training, and the use of part-time instructors with insufficient qualifications. Flexner's recommendations were bold and transformative. He proposed that admission to medical school should require, at a minimum, a high school diploma and at least two years of college education focused on basic sciences. At the time, only 16 out of 155 medical schools in the United States and Canada required applicants to have completed two or more years of university education. By 1920, 92% of U.S. medical schools had adopted this requirement. Flexner also recommended that medical education should last four years, with a curriculum aligned with the CME's 1905 standards. He advocated for the closure or incorporation of proprietary medical schools into universities, as standalone medical schools would need to charge prohibitively high tuition to remain financially viable. Additionally, Flexner suggested appointing full-time clinical professors who would focus on teaching and research rather than private practice. Flexner's vision for medical education was heavily influenced by his exposure to European medical education, particularly the rigorous standards in continental Europe. He demanded that American medical education conform to these prevailing practices. Over time, medical schools in the United States and Canada largely adopted Flexner's recommendations, leading to a standardized, science-based approach to medical education. The Flexner Report also had significant consequences for the diversity of the medical profession. The closure of proprietary medical schools, which often admitted women, African Americans, and students of limited financial means, made medical education more expensive and less accessible to these groups. As a result, the medical profession became dominated by upper-middle-class white males. The report's recommendations also delegitimized existing women doctors and doctors of color, who often continued to practice under challenging circumstances and for lower pay. The report's impact extended to osteopathic medicine and other alternative medical practices, such as naturopathy, homeopathy, and eclectic medicine. Flexner dismissed these approaches as unscientific and recommended that medical schools offering such courses either eliminate them or lose accreditation. Osteopathic medical schools, in particular, were expected to meet the same standards as allopathic schools. Over time, osteopathic and allopathic medical training converged, with osteopathic schools adopting evidence-based, scientific curricula while retaining instruction in manipulative medicine. The Flexner Report is remembered for creating a single, standardized model of medical education that emphasized rigorous scientific training. While it succeeded in raising the quality of medical education and practice, it also contributed to the reduction of diversity within the medical profession and made access to medical care more challenging for underserved populations. The report's legacy continues to shape medical education and practice in the United States and Canada to this day.
